stories.headline: JUNE CPI POSTS BIGGEST MONTHLY DROP SINCE 2020, SENDING S&P 500 TO 7,543.59 AND YIELDS LOWER
stories.body: Headline CPI fell 0.4% in June — the largest one-month decline since April 2020 — pulling the annual rate to 3.5% versus the 3.8% economists expected, as energy prices dropped 5.7%. The S&P 500 rose 0.38% to 7,543.59 and the Nasdaq-100 jumped 1.07% to roughly 29,578, led by a semiconductor rally in SK Hynix and Micron, while the 10-year Treasury yield fell 2 basis points to 4.58% and the 2-year slid 7 basis points to about 4.19%.
stories.explain: CPI measures the average price level households paid during June, so a sharp drop in the energy component — gasoline and utility costs that had already been falling from their spring peak — mechanically pulls the headline number down even though core inflation (ex-food and energy) was flat, not negative. The bigger 2-year yield move versus the 10-year reflects that short rates track the Fed's near-term policy path most directly, so traders read a cooler print as reducing hike odds at the July 29 FOMC meeting, while the 10-year's smaller decline shows longer-run inflation expectations barely budged. That gap is also why this print is backward-looking: it can't capture the oil spike that hit later the same day, which is exactly today's Deep Dive.

stories.headline: OIL JUMPS TO A ONE-MONTH HIGH AS U.S. REIMPOSES A HORMUZ BLOCKADE AND IRAN STRIKES TWO UAE TANKERS
stories.body: Brent crude settled up 1.72% at $84.73 a barrel after trading as high as $87 intraday, and WTI rose about 2.0% to $79.56, after the U.S. launched fresh airstrikes on Iran and reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports and coastal areas at 4 p.m. ET. Iran retaliated by striking two Abu Dhabi National Oil Company tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, killing one mariner; separately, Trump dropped his earlier proposal for a 20% U.S.-military-protection toll on ships crossing the strait.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil flow, so any strike that damages an actual tanker — rather than just threatening one — forces traders to reprice the probability of a sustained supply disruption rather than a symbolic escalation, which is why oil jumped more sharply today than during earlier rounds of this conflict. Brent, the global benchmark loaded via tankers that would transit Hormuz, is more directly exposed to a chokepoint closure than WTI, which is largely landlocked U.S. pipeline crude — a structural reason Brent has been outpricing WTI through this escalation. Watch tanker insurance rates and actual transit volumes, not just headlines, to see whether this premium sticks or fades like the earlier scare.

stories.headline: IBM CRATERS 25% IN ITS WORST DAY EVER AFTER A SECOND-QUARTER REVENUE WARNING TIED TO ITS NEW MAINFRAME
stories.body: IBM shares plunged roughly 25% — surpassing its prior record decline of 23.7% from October 19, 1987 — after preliminary Q2 results missed expectations, with adjusted EPS of $2.93 on $17.2 billion in revenue versus consensus of $3.01 and $17.86 billion. Management pointed to a shortfall in its software and infrastructure business tied to the rollout of its new z17 mainframe, as clients shifted late-June capex toward servers, storage, and memory to lock in supply-constrained AI infrastructure ahead of expected price increases.
stories.explain: A pre-announced 'shortfall' before the official earnings date signals management has enough visibility into the quarter's numbers to know a miss is coming and would rather get ahead of it than let a surprise land on the scheduled report date — that urgency itself is a negative signal independent of the numbers. The mechanism here is a capex-timing reallocation, not lost demand: enterprise clients diverted dollars earmarked for IBM's z17 mainframes toward AI-adjacent hardware they feared would get more expensive or supply-constrained, meaning the revenue may show up in a future quarter rather than vanishing outright. That distinction is why the stock cratered on the miss itself rather than any read-through to broader enterprise IT demand, which is a big reason the Nasdaq-100 still closed up over 1% the same day.

stories.headline: GOLD CLIMBS TOWARD $4,090 AS A SOFTER DOLLAR AND HORMUZ RISK COMPOUND
stories.body: Gold rose roughly 1.4% to about $4,092 an ounce, rebounding from Monday's 2.9% slide to a one-week low near $4,001, as the dollar index dropped about 0.5% to 100.74 on the cooler CPI print and Iran-driven safe-haven demand added a second tailwind.
stories.explain: Gold is getting a rare double push today: a weaker dollar mechanically makes gold cheaper for foreign buyers and lowers the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset as rate-cut odds rise, while the Hormuz escalation is pulling in safe-haven flows independent of the dollar move. When both drivers point the same direction the price response tends to be larger than either alone would produce, which is part of why gold's rebound today outpaced Monday's slide in percentage terms. The tell for which driver dominates going forward is whether gold keeps rising if the dollar stabilizes — that would mean geopolitical risk, not rates, is now doing the driving.

stories.headline: NCAA MEN'S TOURNAMENT WILL EXPAND TO 76 TEAMS FOR 2026-27 AS RECRUITING RESHUFFLES THE TOP CLASSES
stories.body: The NCAA confirmed the Division I men's basketball tournament will grow from 68 to 76 teams starting in 2026-27, with the women's tournament expanding the same way. On the recruiting trail, Texas jumped into the top-five class rankings after 6-foot-10 forward Marcus Spears reclassified from 2027 to sign with the Longhorns over Arizona, LSU and Kentucky, while Kansas landed the 2026 class' top overall prospect, guard Tyran Stokes.

stories.headline: GRIZZLIES TRADE JA MORANT TO THE TRAIL BLAZERS AS SUMMER LEAGUE ROLLS ON IN VEGAS
stories.body: Former All-Star guard Ja Morant is headed from Memphis to Portland in a trade, one of the offseason's biggest moves, while the Wizards are finalizing a three-year, $17.6 million sign-and-trade deal for wing Khris Middleton. In Las Vegas, the Rockets held the 76ers to 31.1% shooting in a 90-64 win to open Tuesday's Summer League slate, and No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson threw down a highlight-reel dunk for New Orleans.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS SALE TO THE KHOSLA FAMILY VALUED AT AN NFL-RECORD $9.612 BILLION AWAITS OWNER VOTE
stories.body: The Estate of Paul G. Allen agreed to sell the Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks to a group led by the Khosla family for a reported $9.612 billion, shattering the prior NFL record of $6.05 billion paid for the Washington Commanders in 2023. The deal needs approval from at least 24 of the NFL's 32 owners at a special meeting expected in late August, and requires the Khosla family to divest its existing minority stake in the San Francisco 49ers.

stories.headline: LSU HEADLINES THE TRANSFER PORTAL CYCLE WITH EIGHT TOP-100 SIGNEES AS THE WINDOW CLOSES
stories.body: College football's transfer portal window for 2026 has effectively closed, with LSU signing eight of ESPN's top 100 transfer prospects under new coach Lane Kiffin, including the No. 1-ranked tackle Jordan Seaton and edge rusher Princewill Umanmielen. Penn State's new coaching staff brought nearly 40 transfers from Iowa State, while Colorado's Deion Sanders rebuilt a 3-9 roster around Texas wide receiver transfer DeAndre Moore Jr.

sports.detail: Agreed to be sold to the Khosla family for an NFL-record $9.612 billion, pending a late-August owner vote. RB Zach Charbonnet is 'progressing well' from his torn ACL ahead of a late-July checkup. Training camp public practices begin July 25 in Renton.

Fell to the Knicks 86-75 in Vegas Summer League Monday — Chaz Lanier led Detroit with 24 points on 8-for-12 shooting from three. Detroit is 2-3 in the tournament after beating Cleveland 103-94 two days earlier. Next: vs. Suns, Wednesday 7/15, 6 PM ET, the Pistons' Summer League finale.

Enter the break at 48-49 — a Wild Card spot, one game behind AL West-leading Texas (49-47) — after snapping a five-game skid with an 8-2 win over Tampa Bay Saturday. LF Randy Arozarena represents Seattle at tonight's All-Star Game in Philadelphia (8 PM ET). Regular season resumes this weekend.

RB Jordan Washington remains on track for a late-July return from the spring injury that carted him off the practice field. Jedd Fisch enters year three with a Big Ten slate featuring road trips to USC, Purdue, Nebraska, Michigan State and Oregon; the season opens September 5 at home against Washington State in the Apple Cup.

UW is one of four finalists for 5-star guard Dylan Mingo as Danny Sprinkle rebuilds through the portal following Zoom Diallo's departure. International signee Nikola Dzepina has joined the program; F Hannes Steinbach, the 14th pick in June's NBA Draft, begins his rookie season with Charlotte.

Strait of Hormuz — U.S. blockade and tanker strikes escalating; watch insurance rates and transit volumes for whether the oil premium sticks
IBM Q2 earnings call — official report date still pending after today's 25% pre-announcement plunge

deepDive.title: The CPI Time Lag: Why Cooling June Inflation and a Surging July Oil Shock Aren't a Contradiction
content: Today's brief holds two facts that look like they should cancel each other out: the June CPI report showed prices fell 0.4% — the sharpest monthly drop since the pandemic — while WTI and Brent crude simultaneously jumped on a fresh U.S.-Iran escalation and a reimposed Hormuz blockade. If oil is a major input into the price of everything from gasoline to shipping, how can inflation be cooling and an oil shock be happening on the very same day? The answer is that CPI is a rearview mirror, not a live feed: the number released this morning describes prices households actually paid during the four weeks of June, a period that ended two weeks before today's tanker strikes and blockade even occurred.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics builds the CPI by sending price checkers and collecting receipts across a full calendar month, then publishes the result with roughly a two-week lag. June's energy index fell 5.7% because oil had been drifting lower through most of that month — nothing in today's report reflects the escalation that began in the report's final days and accelerated well after the survey window closed. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy specifically because those categories are volatile and geopolitically reactive, was flat in June, which is arguably the more useful read on underlying inflation trend precisely because it isn't distorted by a single month's oil swing in either direction.

This lag matters because markets don't wait for the data to catch up — they price expectations forward through instruments like TIPS breakevens and oil futures curves, which is why WTI and Brent moved within hours of the blockade news while CPI won't reflect any of it until the July report releases in mid-August. The 1990 Gulf War is the classic case study: oil spiked over 100% in the months after Iraq invaded Kuwait, but headline CPI didn't fully capture the inflationary hit until two to three months later, by which point the Fed was already behind the curve on a shock that markets had priced almost immediately. The lag isn't a flaw in the CPI methodology — it's an inherent feature of measuring realized prices rather than expected ones, and it's exactly why the Fed increasingly leans on market-based and survey-based inflation expectations alongside the official print.

For the July 29 FOMC meeting, this means today's cooler CPI print is genuine near-term relief — it's why the 2-year yield fell 7 basis points, the most Fed-sensitive maturity, more than the 10-year's 2 basis points — but it is not a clean read on where inflation is headed if Hormuz stays disrupted through July. If tanker traffic keeps falling and oil holds near today's levels into month-end, the energy component of the July CPI report, due in mid-August, could reverse sharply higher, arriving right as markets are digesting whatever the Fed decides on July 29 with only the stale June data in hand. The gap between what CPI says today and what oil markets are pricing right now is the exact spread investors get paid to trade — and exactly what the Fed has to guess at three weeks before the actual data can confirm it either way.
